analysis.one_liner: Lets student loan borrowers refinance at 2013 rates, paid for by a 30% minimum tax on millionaires.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a House vote: referred to two committees in May 2014, sent to a subcommittee in June, and it died there when the 113th Congress ended, despite 142 Democratic cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would let people who took out student loans before mid-2013 — federal loans, older bank-backed FFEL loans, and private student loans — refinance them at the lower fixed rates that applied in the 2013-14 school year (about 3.9% for undergraduate loans, versus the 6.8% many older loans carried). To pay for it, anyone earning over $1 million a year would pay a minimum 30% tax on that income. The program would shut down once the tax money collected covered its cost.
analysis.who_benefits: Millions of former students still repaying loans taken out before July 2013, especially those paying older, higher rates. Federal and FFEL borrowers meeting income tests could refinance at the 2013-14 rates and keep their repayment timelines; borrowers in the greatest financial need would get priority. Borrowers with high-interest private loans could move into cheaper fixed-rate federal loans.

how_it_helps.text: Qualified borrowers could reissue federal Direct Loans, older bank-backed FFEL loans, and private student loans at the lower fixed interest rates that applied for the 12 months starting July 1, 2013, with the new rate locked for the life of the loan.
Eligibility would be set by income or debt-to-income, with rules written to give first access to borrowers with the greatest financial need.

Borrowers would keep their original repayment term — the bill explicitly bars extending the repayment period — and payments made on the original loan would still count toward income-based repayment and, for federal refinances, public service forgiveness.
The refinancing program is designed to be deficit-neutral: it terminates when its net cost equals the extra revenue raised by the 30% minimum tax on incomes over $1 million.

analysis.who_pays: Households with adjusted gross income over $1 million would pay a new 30% minimum tax on income above that threshold (less a charitable contribution deduction), starting in 2015 and adjusted for inflation. Private student loan lenders would lose interest income as borrowers pay them off and refinance into cheaper federal loans. Refinancing borrowers would pay a small fee: up to 0.5% on federal/FFEL refinances and the standard federal origination fee on private-loan refinances.

drawbacks.text: Refinanced private loans would not qualify for any loan forgiveness program, including public service and teacher forgiveness, and payments made before refinancing would not count toward forgiveness or the income-based repayment clock — a real penalty for a borrower who later enters public service.

Refinancing is not automatic or universal: the Education Secretary would set income and debt-to-income limits targeting borrowers with the greatest financial need, and the program must shut down once the millionaires' tax revenue covers its cost, so some willing borrowers could be turned away.
Borrowers pay for the deal: an administrative fee of up to 0.5% on refinanced federal and FFEL loans and the standard federal origination fee on refinanced private loans.

The good-faith objection to the financing: a 30% minimum tax on incomes above $1 million raises rates on a small group of high earners whose income is already taxed, and critics argue such a surcharge discourages investment; the bill also addresses the interest already owed on old loans, not the underlying cost of college for future students.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For borrowers, the benefit is direct and large: shaving several percentage points off the rate on years of remaining payments can save thousands of dollars per year of repayment. The costs are real but narrow — a small fee for borrowers, lost interest income for private lenders, and a higher minimum tax on roughly the top 0.2% of households. The design has genuine flaws: private-loan refinancers give up forgiveness benefits, eligibility is capped by need, and the program self-terminates when the tax money runs out. On balance, a substantial benefit to ordinary borrowers financed by a narrow tax on very high incomes.

outcome.mechanism: Referred to two House committees in May 2014 and to a subcommittee in June; no hearing, markup, or floor vote ever came, and it died when the 113th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. John Tierney introduced the bill on May 6, 2014, joined by 21 original cosponsors.
The House referred it to the Education and the Workforce Committee and the Ways and Means Committee, splitting it between two committees with no set timeline.
On June 13, 2014, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Higher Education and Workforce Training — the last action the bill ever received.
142 House Democrats cosponsored the bill; no Republican cosponsor appears in the record.
The bill never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote before the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015, killing it.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The people better off because the bill died are the households earning over $1 million, who avoid a new 30% minimum tax, and private student loan lenders, who keep the high interest payments the bill would have let borrowers refinance away. Student borrowers got nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: High earners and private loan lenders

for.name: President Barack Obama
for.what_they_did: Publicly backed student loan refinancing paid for by a tax on high incomes in 2014.

sides.party_line_note: All 142 cosponsors were House Democrats and no Republican signed on, so the bill never reached the floor where a partisan vote split could have been recorded.

industries.note: The bill would let borrowers with current private student loans pay them off with cheaper fixed-rate federal loans, moving interest income from private lenders to the federal loan program. Lenders keep their high rates only if the bill fails.

industries.industry: FFEL loan holders and guaranty agencies
industries.note: The bill would buy borrowers out of the old bank-backed FFEL system by paying lenders off and reissuing the loans as federal Direct Loans, ending that interest stream.

industries.industry: Households earning over $1 million a year
industries.note: A new 30% minimum tax on income above $1 million — after a charitable contribution deduction — would fall entirely on this group and is the bill's sole funding source.
Moving old FFEL and private loans into the federal Direct Loan system would enlarge the federal portfolio that federal loan servicers administer, adding servicing volume.
